notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0149b.stoa010.opp-l: The heading's 'INTERPBETATIO', 'ediLis', 'lndidem' are scanning errors for interpretatio, editis, Indidem. In §1 'Marc. xv, 26' and in §3 'Gal. n, 11' are the edition's references (the Galatians quotation is 2:14). In §5 the edition prints 'venit (f. vivit)'; the conjecture 'vivit' (lives) is translated. In §6 'infimis' (to the lowliest) may be corrupt; 'in se', 'tuea' read as 'tuas'. In §2 the 'quid... habet gloriam' passage is loosely constructed and may be corrupt.

§8: the Romans reference printed as 'vn, 33' is Rom. 8:33. 'Deus qui justificat?' follows the punctuation of the edition. §9: 'renes' rendered literally as 'kidneys' (the inward parts). §10: the Romans citation printed as 'VII, 12' corresponds to Rom. 7:22-23; Matthew reference 'xxxvi' read as 26; Psalm 'uv' read as 54 (Vulgate). §11: 'quæ sit istius dextrae sinistra' rendered as 'what is the left of this right'.

Line 12: 'Quis viderit secundum carnem, tentationes introeuntes ad fidem?' is obscure; read as 'Quid viderit'. 'anniuiliaret' read as 'annuntiaret'. Line 14: 'benedicit' read as 'bene dicit' (rightly says). Line 16: 'Ansdayan' is evidently a garbled transliteration of Greek ἀνομίαν (anomia). The sentence beginning 'Facimus enim ignoranter' is awkward and may be corrupt. Line 17: 'non est recte justus a Domino' seems defective; 'ad Dominum' with a verb of approaching understood. 'frnctus (f. finctus)': the edition's conjecture presumably intends 'fluctus' (waves), followed here. 'adaperliomun' read as 'revelationum' (2 Cor. 12:7).

Psalm verses are given in the Vulgate numbering of the text (Ps. 31 and 41 = Hebrew 32 and 42). In the Ps. 41 opening, the reference '(Num. 12:8)' printed after 'sons of Korah' appears misplaced; the Korah rebellion is Num. 16. 'vitem habui' (twice) read as 'vilem habui', 'held it cheap'. 'in cilium vitæ æternæ' read as 'in cibum', 'for food'. 'imperia' read with the edition's marginal correction 'improperia', 'reproaches'. 'certus' read throughout as 'cervus', 'deer'. Line 3: 'Multa flagella peccatoris' is verse 10, though the text marks it verse 9. The Luke reference printed as 'xvii, 55' should be 17:33.

Line 26: 'sub pedibus' corrected (as the edition suggests) to 'sub pellibus', 'under the skins'. The Ps. 83:2 citation is elliptical; 'tabernacula tua' is evidently implied. Line 29: in the Song 4:8 quotation 'ab initio fidei' reflects the Latin rendering of 'Amana' (taken as 'faith'); the final sentence ('quibus Filius Dei creditur operatus') is awkwardly constructed and the rendering is approximate.

Line 1: the 'foolish woman' suggests Job's wife, but the words cited (Job 22:3) belong to Eliphaz; the quotation is loose. 'vetice' read as 'vertice' (summit). Line 3: 'quasi In nos ita frequenter ... qua? caro emergat, quæ caro sustineat?' seems corrupt; rendered tentatively. 'recent' read as 'fecerit'. Line 4: Ps. 'XII. 17' is evidently Ps. 21:17 (Vulgate); 'actio' read as 'aceto'. Line 5: numbered '15' in the scan, evidently 13. 'Inter diem' read as 'interdiu' (by day). 'nisi sit tempus causa miserandi' is obscure, perhaps corrupt; the bracketed [not] is a conjecture. The sentence beginning 'tunc si potuerimus dicere' has no main clause in the text. The verse is quoted first with 'oblitus es' (forgotten), then with 'dereliquisti' (forsaken). Line 6: 'dum confringis' (while you break) may be a corruption of 'dum confringuntur'.

nodes.text: SAINT HILARY'S [INTERPRETATION OF] PSALMS 15, 31 AND 41
INTERPRETATION, which has hitherto been lacking in the editions. (From the same [source].) TRACTATE ON PSALM 15.

1. This psalm is headed with the inscription of a title; but what the inscription of David's title was, we do not find in the history. Nevertheless we recognise the inscription of a title made at the passion of the Lord; and it cannot be denied, according to interpretation, that this psalm appears to have prophesied about the passion and resurrection of Christ, which is plain in the place where it says (verse 10): For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you let your holy one see corruption. For David died and was buried; but the flesh of Christ alone did not see corruption, nor could his soul be held in hell. Therefore the psalm, which was going to speak of his passion and resurrection and inheritance, was rightly marked with the inscription of a title. For what did the writing of the title contain which Pilate fixed to his cross? Jesus, it says, king of the Jews. This name he himself also acknowledged as his, when Pilate asked him: Are you the king of the Jews? (Mark 15:26). For this, he says, I came, and for this I was born.

2. But was he [made] king of the carnal Jews by him upon Sion, his holy mountain? I certainly do not think that the kingdom given to the Lord by the Father is on this earthly mountain which is in Judaea, the Lord whose kingdom the Apostle teaches is heavenly; just as he shows that the city of Jerusalem itself which belongs to Christ is not this one which is now in slavery with her children, but that which is above, our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem. So too [he is king] not of these Jews who are circumcised with a circumcision made by hand, but as the Apostle taught, saying: that he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is in the flesh, but the circumcision of the heart, whose praise is not from men but from God; and Jesus is not the king of those Jews who glory before men on account of works, but of those whose glory is before God because of the hope of his grace. For see the Apostle saying whose glory is before God. For if, he says, Abraham was justified by works, he has glory before men (Rom. 4:2); why does he believe in him who is able to justify the ungodly, and hope for the free mercy of God? He has glory, but not before God.

3. Christ, then, is king of the Jews whose glory is not from men but from God. Accordingly this psalm too says pointedly (verses 5 and 6): The Lord is the portion of my inheritance. The lines have fallen for me in the most powerful [places], for my inheritance is very great indeed. What, then, is the inheritance of the Lord, if not that of which it is written: Ask, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance (Ps. 2:8)? Now sinners from the nations believe in him who is able to justify the ungodly. And if their glory is not from men but from God, Christ is also the king of these Jews. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is done openly in the flesh. But what does he say? Did not very many from that circumcision believe? It is true that they believed, but they too were brought back to the pattern of the gentiles, so that they first confessed themselves sinners, and so earned mercy, as Paul teaches when writing to the Galatians: If you, he says, though you are a Jew, live like a gentile, how do you compel the gentiles to judaize? (Gal. 2:14). We are Jews by nature and not sinners from the gentiles, knowing that no flesh is justified by the law. And so, wishing to be gained in Christ, he was found a sinner; because Christ came to call not the justified but sinners. So those too who believed from the circumcision made by hand believed when humbled to the confession of the sinful gentiles, so that all might be the inheritance of Christ: not among those who will be justified by their own works, but among those who are justified through the free grace of God. And this is the inscription of the title, that he himself is king of the Jews. So this psalm tells of which Jews Christ is seen to be king, and what reason it has for the inscription of the title; he is [king] not of those Jews who are seen outwardly, and whose circumcision is open in the flesh, but rather of those Jews who are Jews in secret, who have circumcision of the heart, whose glory is not from men but from God. Let us then see the text of the psalm, whether it bears on what we have said.

4. Verse 1. Keep me, it says, Lord, for in you I have hoped. One who asks for what is owed does not hope: for if something is owed to me, I demand it back by right. But if someone gives me something of his own will, not as an offering, from this habit of his I will hope for his kindness. So this man, who did not exalt righteousness from works but brought in the free grace of God, said: Keep me, Lord, for in you I have hoped. I will say to the Lord: You are my God. For the power of a lord lies in this, that he does to his servant what he wishes, not what he is obliged to. But if a wage is owed for works, he will pay me back what he is obliged to, not what he wishes. For if I have worked, willing or not, the wage is owed to me, and by this the grace of God will be made void, as the Apostle says: For to one who works, the wage is reckoned as a debt, not as grace; but one who wishes to be saved not by his own works but by the grace of God, as we all ought to believe, he, hoping in God, will establish for himself the good which God wishes, not what he is obliged to; and for this reason he says pointedly (verse 2): I said to the Lord, You are my God. For a lord never thanks a servant if he has done what he commanded; but through all these things he will want his kindness and grace to be awaited, as the Lord too teaches, saying: Which of you has a servant ploughing or pasturing? When he comes home, does he say to him, Come over and recline? No, he says, Come over and serve me, and then you shall eat. Does the master thank that servant because he did so? Amen I say to you, he does not. So you too, when you have done all that I command you, say: We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do (Luke 17:7). Therefore whoever acknowledges that he has God ought to show such humility of servitude. But this confession is not of works but of faith. So the herald of the New Testament well says: I said to my Lord, You are my God. And what does he say after this?

5. For you do not need my goods, (verse 3) to the saints who are on the earth. What could follow more naturally than his saying that his goods are not necessary to the saints of the earth, and that those goods of the Lord are not for the use of the saints who inhabit the earth? And what are the goods of Christ, what the goods of the New Testament, if not free [gifts], if not the remission of sins? These goods are not necessary to the saints of the earth. Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill (Mark 2:17). And properly he called those who justify themselves in their works saints not of heaven but of earth; for their praise is from men, not from God: such the Lord marks them out to have been, justifying themselves in the sight of men, when to those who blamed him for eating with tax collectors he said: I did not come to save the righteous, but sinners (ibid.). Therefore free grace and the remission of sins are not necessary to the righteous; but, of course, to the righteous who think themselves righteous; for the truly righteous lives by faith. So these saints have no need of the goods of his son. So below he says: I will not gather their synagogues from my blood. For redemption through my blood is not necessary for such people, who think themselves righteous.

6. But why does he say: They made your wills wonderful in themselves; (verse 4) their infirmities were multiplied: after this they hastened? The Apostle treats this place most fully in Romans, that the law came in so that sin might be increased. Where sin was increased, there grace abounded (Rom. 5:20). For after they were found, having rejected the grace of God, in the works of the law, the will of God, by which he called them to his grace, was made wonderful to the lowliest. Whoever, then, wishes to be saved must wish to be set free by the grace of God. So the psalm well says: They made your wills wonderful in themselves; their infirmities were multiplied: after this they hastened. For when the infirmities of those who wished to be justified by works were multiplied, the wills of God which called them to the faith of grace were made wonderful. Their synagogues, then, he says, I will not gather from my blood: that is, I will not redeem those who do not seek the redemption of my grace. Nor, he says, will I remember their names through your lips. For one who wishes to be saved by his own works does not confess my kindness: and whoever does not confess me before men, I will not confess him before my Father who is in heaven (Matt. 10:32). But if he was not going to gather such people, it remained for him to show whom he would receive as his inheritance. So in due order he adds:

7. Verse 5. The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one who kept my inheritance there. For if he rejected those who are justified by works, he certainly preferred to have those whom God was saving through grace. So he says pointedly: The Lord is the portion of my inheritance. For since the Lord by his grace has saved those whom he gave [him] as an inheritance, truly the Lord is the portion of his inheritance. And the son kept to obedience, so as not to proclaim his inheritance as gained by his own blood, but to say that it was given to him by God through God, so that he confesses the Lord to be the portion of his cup too, that is, of his passion. For if the nations were redeemed from sin by the passion of the Lord, yet the passion of the Lord itself was the will of the Father, as he testifies in the gospel, saying (as the man speaks whom he took up): Father, let this cup pass from me: yet not what I will, but what you [will] (Matt. 26:39). Therefore if you consider the will of the Lord, he himself confessed it, saying: If it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Hence also the redemption of the nations is to be taken as lying not in the will of the Son, but in the will of the Father. For not what I will, he says, but what you [will]. Therefore this very grace by which the nations were redeemed through his death the Son assigns not to himself but to the Father. So he asserts that the Lord is the portion both of his inheritance and of his cup.

8. Verse 6. The lines, he says, have fallen to me among the most mighty: for my inheritance is very great to me. For it was an old custom that the boundaries of possessions were measured with a line: and so here, since he was speaking of the portion of his inheritance, he says, The lines have fallen to me among the most mighty themselves. And we receive testimony of this matter from the song of Moses, where it is written: When God dispersed the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and his people became the portion of the Lord, Jacob the line of his inheritance (Deut. 32:8). And rightly he who had said that God was the portion of his inheritance said that the lines of his possession had fallen among the most mighty themselves. For who are most mighty, if not those whom the Lord justifies, whom the Lord honours? Who will accuse the elect of God? God who justifies? Who has condemned (Rom. 8:33)? Therefore he who said that his inheritance would be among such people rightly says: The lines have fallen to me among the most mighty themselves. But as for his saying that they fell, let no one take it as though he were calling his inheritance worse, because everything that falls becomes worse; rather he used a proper and necessary word. For where someone is chosen not on account of merit, there a kind of lot of grace, as it were, falls; as in the taking up of the apostle who was put in the place of Judas, it is written that the lot fell upon Matthias (Acts 1:26). So, because such an inheritance had come to him only from the grace of the Lord, he says pointedly: The lines have fallen to me among the most mighty themselves: for my inheritance is very great to me. Here the new Adam speaks.

9. Verse 7. I will bless the Lord who made me understand: for the Son knows nothing except what he has seen and heard from the Father. So he blesses him who made him understand. And truly this understanding is not from man but from God. For which of men, when two inheritances are set before him, one magnificent and rich in works, the other poor and needy, would choose the one that needs another's mercy? But the Son, taught by the Father, prefers an inheritance among those who hope in God rather than among those who are justified by their own works. So he says beautifully: I will bless the Lord who made me understand; and moreover, as in the night, my kidneys instructed me. What did his kidneys instruct him? Namely, he says, they made him understand that it is better to hope in the Lord than to be justified by one's own work. For did not his kidneys, as in the night, instruct the Lord himself too to hope in God? For his soul too was sorrowful even to death. He learned to hope in God, and this is what he means by saying he was instructed in this understanding by his kidneys, as in the night. For what follows also shows that he is speaking of his passion, when he adds:

10. Verses 8-10. I foresaw the Lord in my sight always, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. Because of this my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted; moreover my flesh too will dwell in hope: for you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you let your holy one see corruption. The wording and order here are clear: but as to his naming the kidneys and saying, as in the night they instructed me, let us inquire, lest these things seem too obscure. God is called the searcher of the kidneys and the heart, in which, as in two places, the secrets of a man are held. But in the heart is the secret of the soul, in the kidneys the secret of the flesh; and the Apostle too teaches these differences between the inner and outer man, when he says: I agree with the law according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind (Rom. 7:22). And in another place: So then I myself serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin (ibid. 25). Such a kind of dissension our Lord Jesus himself also reports that he feels, where he says: The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak: for according to the inner man he agreed with the law of the Father, to suffer; but according to the outer, as he himself testifies, he trembled in the flesh. So, because the kidneys contain the secrets of the flesh, which was weak at the time of the passion, he says he was instructed by his kidneys, so that he himself, though he was the Son, should understand how to hope in God. And the letter written to the Hebrews thinks likewise about him. For although, it says, he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things he suffered: and being made perfect he became for all who obey [him] the cause of eternal salvation (Heb. 5:8). For thus the kidneys instructed him to foresee God at his right hand always, so that he might not be moved. That is, as to the will, the spirit is willing, but the flesh weak. And properly he said that he was instructed by his kidneys as in the night; he did not say in night, but as in the night. For his senses were not wholly darkened by the fear of death, since he said: Yet not what I will, but what you [will] (Matt. 26:39). But still he was not without some disturbance, since he confessed weakness and sorrow. For if elsewhere David says: The fear of death fell upon me, fear and trembling seized me, and darkness covered me (Ps. 54:6); rightly this darkness, coming from the fear of death, which it is fitting should have been very slight in the Son of God, is called not night but as it were night. So it is said pointedly: And moreover, as in the night, my kidneys instructed me. And what did they instruct? Namely what follows below: that he should foresee God in his sight always, because he is at his right hand, so that he might not be moved.

11. For this, he says, my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted; moreover my flesh too will dwell in hope: since you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you let your holy one see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life: you will fill me with gladness with your countenance: delights are in your right hand. So the joys too are in the right hand of God, with all of which the Son is filled. For he had God at his right. I foresaw the Lord, he says, in my sight always, for he is at my right hand. And ascending into heaven, he himself came to be at the right hand of the Father. At his right hand: let us ask what is the left of this right. In a certain place, then, the Apostle knows weapons of righteousness on the right and the left, namely glory and dishonour. By the right I take the form of righteousness; but by the left dishonour and infamy. Yet both are weapons of righteousness. But to come to the right-hand weapons of righteousness, we must first serve as soldiers with the left. For in this world dishonour, infamy, weakness, foolishness and the like must be taken up, so that we may come to nobility, to glory, to power, to wisdom: all of which we shall receive when we have come there where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. We are sown in dishonour, that we may rise in glory; we are sown in mortality, that we may rise into eternity. So our Lord, having suffered at the time of his passion the mockery of scourges and of spittle, when he was accused as a blasphemer, when he was reckoned among robbers, placed in such dishonour and infamy, what else was he doing but fighting with the left-hand weapons of righteousness? So, placed then on the left of God, he foresaw him at his right hand, so that he might not be moved. But after he rose again and ascended into heaven, coming to the right hand, to the palm of righteousness, to glory, to nobility, he is filled with gladness with the countenance of God, and has delights in his right hand. Toward these the Apostle encourages us in hope, saying: For the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with those good things to come which will be revealed in us (Rom. 8:18). For this reason let us too glory the more gladly in our weaknesses, that the power of God may protect us. And now may the Father be at our right hand, so that we may not be moved, he who will afterwards transfer us to his right hand, into the riches of our Lord Jesus Christ: to whom be glory. Amen.
TRACTATE ON PSALM 31.

1. *A psalm of David, of understanding*: [this title] marks the prophecy that it contains. The Apostle taught that it announced the New Testament through the calling of the gentiles. In this [Testament] faith was to be justified without works, and in it there was promised the future remission of iniquities and forgetting of sins through the free grace of God; and the reasoning for this is plain. But it is worth while to go through the whole text of the psalm, in which the feelings of the psalmist may be discerned. What did he see, according to the flesh, as temptations come in upon faith? For he saw that those are blessed whose righteousness was not reckoned from works. For the law came in so that sins might be increased; and the law produces wrath; and where there is no law, there is no transgression either. Therefore he will not undeservedly be called blessed who was not under the law, but rather under grace.

2. But what kind of faith is required, the psalmist marked by saying, verse 2: *And no deceit has been found in his mouth.* I believe he is surely seeking such a man as Nathanael, whom the Lord praised as he came to him; such as were not those in Israel whom God had thus rebuked through the prophets: *This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me* (Isa. 29:13). Nor is there any doubt that this is deceit: to have one thing on the lips, another in the heart. So David rightly says in another psalm: *I believed, therefore I spoke* (Ps. 115:10). And the Apostle explains: that with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). So if someone believes in the heart what the lips confess, no deceit will be found in his mouth. But if someone honours God with the lips, but his heart is found far from him, there is deceit in his mouth; and we are properly marked by this at the time when we follow the teachings of men and our own counsels, rejecting the commandments of God. For so it is written: *This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far* (Isa. 29:13). *They worship me, following the commandments and teachings of men* (Matt. 15:7). So too the Lord in the Gospel calls the teachers of the law hypocrites, passing over the will of God and setting up their own counsels. And every hypocrite is a pretender and is deceitful. And certainly it is plain deceit to promise faith to God and to trust in human counsels. Men of this kind can neither remit iniquities nor cover sins, because they place their salvation in the counsels of men rather than in the help of God. Then the prophet marks, as it were, his own temptation at once in the wavering of faith; and as if chastising himself, he warns what others ought to avoid, saying that when the hand of God had been heavy upon him, that is, persisting in many temptations, he did indeed cry out to God, but did not persevere in the crying; rather at last he fell silent, and from the silence his bones at once grew old.

3. What we should understand spiritually by bones we have often noted: that just as bones are the support and strength of one's body, so patience is the support and strength of our mind. So this man, who, when the hand of God was heavy upon him, could not persevere towards God, but failed and fell silent, rightly says that his bones grew old: that is, that his patience aged. And all old age brings weakness. So it is also plain that his patience was weakened. And he properly put 'grew old', that is, returned to the old impatience; for the new man and the new birth have persevering patience. Hence the Apostle says: *Tribulation will produce patience, patience proof, proof hope; and hope does not confound, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts* (Rom. 5:3). Therefore, since in the new man the love of God has been poured out in the heart through the Holy Spirit, who cries: *Abba, Father*, his patience rightly perseveres, so that he can say: *Who will separate me from the love of God? Tribulation, distress, or nakedness, or famine, or the sword?* (Rom. 8:35). But he who failed in crying and hoping in God rightly says that his bones grew old; that is, they returned to the old impatience, since the love of the new birth failed, which never despairs of the Father.

4. What then does he teach? That this is a faithful promise to us: that if [there is] iniquity or the working of sin, even if the hand of the Lord has become heavy upon us and has burdened us with many temptations, our cry to God ought not to fail. What if we fall silent? [It means] that we return to our old thoughts, seeking a remedy in our own counsels, applying cares and anxieties, and through our own wisdom abandoning the hope that is from God, which is firmer than all our thoughts. And the prophet, marking this as in temptation, sings, verses 3 and 4: *Because I was silent, all my bones grew old; when I had cried out all day and night, your hand was heavy upon me.* And what does he say last? *I was turned into misery, while a thorn was fixed in me.* Thus he plainly signifies that from this fault, that in the temptations that came upon him he had ceased to cry to God and to hope, as silence and speechlessness followed, he took up in his thoughts the cares and anxieties of his life, and through this was turned into misery, having abandoned, that is, the hope of God's help; and he says pointedly that a thorn was fixed in him. For the Lord teaches in the Gospel that thorns are the cares and anxieties of livelihood, by which the word is choked; and this thorn, that is, care and anxiety about life, the prophet here says was fixed in him from the time he fell silent and ceased to cry to God, through which he confesses he was turned into misery. And since these worldly cares and anxieties often creep into our minds even when they are not noticed, he says: *Make my sin known to me.*

5. And he made a separation, distinguishing iniquity from sin; for iniquity can by no means be unknown. The meaning of this word is more apt in Greek. For they call it *anomia* [lawlessness], by which is signified the time in which the world lived without law, when, still in gentile life, it did not know God. And all who are converted to the Lord must confess that the life of the former time was damnable. But since we define the name of sin as that by which someone enters into the cares and anxieties and thoughts of livelihood, which are so many and various, and whose images so often present themselves even to the good against their will, who could detect them by his own watchfulness? So on this the prophet rightly seeks help from God, saying, verse 5: *Make my sin known to me, Lord.* And we plainly find that the name of sin is held in this [sense] from the beginning of the world, if we examine the very transgression of the first-formed man. But it would take long to pursue this; yet the senses distinguishing between sin and iniquity are equally made plain to those who follow [the text] further. For concerning sin he asks that it be made known to him; but of iniquity he says that he has not concealed it. For as to the latter, since it did not exist without a man's knowledge, there remained in it the medicine of humility, that he should declare it and confess it to the Lord. But sin, whose variety could creep up even on one unaware, whose multitude could deceive and lie hidden, he prayed should be made known to him. Then he persisted in the meaning of the word; and since he was separating iniquity from sin, he said: *I*, he says, *will declare against myself my iniquity, Lord.* So here too [he does not say] 'I will declare my sin, Lord', but iniquity. For he could not declare sin, the knowledge of which he was seeking for himself from the Lord. But iniquity, which he had in his conscience, this, he says, I will declare against myself before the Lord. For there is no other medicine for iniquity except confession to God. For we act in ignorance [in] what the Lord makes known, when conversion has brought about recognition of it, and repentance must follow. So after this iniquity, if he has confessed before the Lord and declared it against himself, that is, having become his own accuser, he will redeem the impiety of his heart. And here with prudent reasoning he says: *I said: I will declare against myself my iniquity, Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart.* Then he who does not confess iniquity to the Lord takes up pride against the Lord, and so acquires impiety. For he does not acknowledge the Lord as father of all creation. On the contrary, the prophet calls humble the one who will confess, and through this prays for pardon of the crime of impiety; which is indeed the opposite of the proud.

6. *For this*, he says, *the humble and righteous will pray to you at the right time.* So there is a time when it is not right for the righteous [to approach] the Lord. The prophet himself teaches this in what follows, saying, verse 6: *But in the flood of many waters they will not come near to him.* So in the flood of many waters it is not the right time for the righteous to come near to the Lord; for it is not for a righteous man to give his soul boldness, as the law also says: *You shall not give your soul boldness.* But if someone seeks the Lord in deep and most lofty mysteries, let him search all his judgements; and if perhaps he thinks he can be equal to withstanding all his waves, this man will not be righteous, nor will he profitably try to come near and seek the Lord in the flood of many waters, since in the exaltation of his own wisdom he has attempted to knock at the hidden things of his depth. So too the apostle Paul: *And lest I be exalted*, he says, *in the abundance of revelations, a goad was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me; for which reason I asked the Lord three times; and it was said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness* (2 Cor. 12:7-9). So here too the prophet, having said that the righteous and humble will not come near to the Lord in the flood of many waters, shows himself at what time the Lord is rather to be sought by him, verse 7: *You are*, he says, *my refuge from the tribulation that surrounds me.* And so he too glories rather in weaknesses, that the power of God may protect him, as Paul says: *So I will more gladly glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may protect me* (ibid. 9). Then he added: *My exultation, free me from those who surround me.* He calls the Lord his exultation, because the wise man should not glory in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength; but let each one glory in this, that he has known and fears the Lord. *My exultation, then, free me from those who surround me.*

7. Verse 8. *I will understand, and I will be joined to you in this way in which you will walk; I will fix my eyes on you.* There follows the precept that is commanded: *You shall walk after the Lord your God.* And this is the faithful man: not to choose a way for himself, but to follow the very way which the Lord shows, and to think right what he has commanded. Then he says: *I will fix my eyes on you*; that is, so that they may look at nothing else except what the Lord directs. He says this more plainly in another psalm: *As the eyes of a handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are on our Lord* (Ps. 122:2); that is, not that we ourselves are directed to aim at the truth, but that the Lord turns our eyes, in whose hands they ought to be; and because it is in his power where he opens our sight and where he closes it.

8. But if anyone does not come of his own accord to this refuge of God, let us learn how the prophet chastises such a man, to whom he compares him, and what he forbids. *Do not become*, he says, verse 9, *like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.* For a man obeys a word and listens to a voice. But those to whom it can be said: *I sought, and there was no man; I called, and there was none who heard* (Isa. 63:5), are of the same kind as the horse and the mule: they must be forced with bit and bridle to go where they do not want to. For this reason the righteous man asks that their stiff neck and hard jaws be softened by torment and force. And the prophet kindly does not want those who do not draw near to the Lord of their own accord to be left to their hardness, but rather demands that they be dragged by whatever punishments, provided that they are saved. So he says: *With bit and bridle draw in the jaws of those who do not draw near to you.*

9. Verse 9 [10]. *Many are the scourges of the sinner.* For through these the Lord works out salvation for sinners; for by inflicting blows and tribulations he teaches the pride of sinners, so that it may grow used to fearing. *But mercy will surround him who hopes in the Lord.* For he whose hope is always in the help of God need not be led by bit or bridle, or rebuked by the scourge, in order to draw near. So his mercy is very close to this man. Therefore, as the prophet says, verse 11: *Rejoice in the Lord, and exult, you righteous, and be glad, all you upright of heart.* Through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
TRACTATE ON PSALM 41.

1. I think the method of exposition to be kept generally in all the psalms is that the title should first be examined, and the whole psalm fitted to it. For no one is so foolish that, having promised to speak about a cedar, he would describe an oak: much less would the Spirit of God, who we believe spoke through the prophet, have marked one thing in the title and said another in the song of the psalm. So in the present case David has certainly sung those things which ought to be an understanding for the sons of Korah: for such is the heading of the psalm. Now we read that the congregation of Korah in the time of Moses murmured against the ordinance of God, so that they strove to usurp and seize for themselves the highest ministry of the priesthood, which Aaron and his sons had received according to the will of God. This vice of covetousness the Apostle marks and warns against, in a way rebuking it: *So I say to you, through the grace that has been given to me, to all of you, not to think beyond measure, more than you ought to think* (Rom. 12:3); *but let each of you think soberly according as the Lord has imparted the measure of faith. For as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same functions, so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and members one of another, having different gifts* (ibid. 4-6). So to one is given ministry, to another prophecy, to another power, to another the word of teaching. But if anyone, wishing to think beyond measure, goes beyond the measure of the Lord's apportionment, he is found in the folly of Korah, and will be called spiritually a son of Korah: and for such as these this psalm, which teaches understanding, will be sung.

2. Verse 2. *As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for the living God.* I think it is not without reason that the springs of waters are set down, when it would have been the obvious thing to say, 'as the deer longs for the waters'; but he preferred to name the springs of waters, that is, the source and beginning of waters, knowing, that is, through spiritual wisdom, which alone knows the roots of trees and the natures of beasts, that even this dumb animal longs not for whatever waters are nearest, but for the very springs of waters, and seeks the cleaner and purer beginnings of streams. By this example he wants us to be reminded that we too should long the more eagerly for the Lord himself, the spring of life and wisdom, who is the head of all. For this is the one spring from which many divisions of spiritual waters are produced, such as healings, prophecies, kinds of tongues, ministries, the word of knowledge, the word of teaching. But even the measures of those nearest us are not to be sought in such a way that through rivalry and contention and discord we neglect our longing for the spring itself. For we neglect him whenever we are unwilling to keep in peace and charity the measure of his division and ordinance. So whoever are found in this pride, shaped in the likeness of the sons of Korah, will be reminded by this psalm to understand rather towards what they ought to direct their longing, as the righteous man says: *As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for the living God.*

3. Verse 3. *When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have become my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day: Where is your God?* But from this very [phrase], *when shall I come and appear*, it is shown to us that it is not to be obtained from close at hand; and unless our tears have been bread to us day and night, the face of the Lord is by no means reached. And the understanding of the sons of Korah ought to follow the order of the teaching, so that it may know that through many tribulations and afflictions and reproaches one comes to the house of God, lest it be exalted in its pride, knowing that power is proved rather in weaknesses, and lest it seize dignity for itself, because the Apostle says: *Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God; but he was humbled, taking the form of a servant, and found in fashion as a man. He emptied himself even to death, the death of the cross* (Phil. 2:5-8); on which, when he was fixed to it, he heard these reproaches: *Where is your God?*, when they said to him in mockery: *Let him come and deliver him* (Matt. 27:43). So the congregation of Korah is taught, as I said, through how many tribulations and tears one approaches the house; these tears the prophet beautifully says were bread to him, that is, for food of eternal life; and it comes in order that he should say in what follows:

4. Verse 5. *These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.* And indeed I think something should first be said here about the meaning of the word, what *I poured out* is. He says he poured out [his soul] for this reason, that he was going to pass over into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God. Now passages even to the house of God are good things of the spirit. So to pour out the soul is the work of good hope: but what do we know of its common usage? That whatever is poured out is cast away and perishes, and is not as safe as when it is kept in a vessel. For this is to pour out: to pour forth outside what you had shut up somewhere. So he who said *I poured out my soul* must be understood to have said nothing else than 'I cast it away and lost it and held it cheap'. How then did he cast it away and lose it for this reason, that he was going to pass over into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God? Unless perhaps the precept of God makes it plain, who says to his disciples: *Whoever saves his soul will lose it; and whoever loses it will save it* (Luke 17:33). And truly he kept the order: for when he had first spoken of tribulations, that his tears had become bread day and night, while it is said to him every day, *Where is your God?*, *These things*, he says, *I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me*: in which he must be understood to have said nothing else than 'I cast it away and lost it and held it cheap'. How then did he cast away his soul to God? For the righteous man knows that whenever tribulations and persecutions and reproaches come upon him for the name of God, the soul must be lost and cast away and held cheap, so that it may be saved in the day of the Lord; and so here too he pointedly shows that he did not pour out his soul because he had despaired of the hope of the life to come, but poured out his soul because he was going to pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. Taught therefore by this psalm, whenever the enemy persecutes us and reproaches us with the name of the Lord, let us pour out our souls to him, ready to lose them so that we may save them: not pouring them out as though we despaired of confidence in God's help, but because we are sure that they will be given back to us, and that we shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.

5. But whatever this place of the wonderful tabernacle may be, in which there will be a passing over even to the house of God, let us now begin to inquire here. In the old books we find the tabernacle made by Moses for the God of Israel, in which the ark of the covenant was kept (Exod. 26:1), and in it all the mysteries were celebrated, and here they first appeared offering sacrifices before the face of God, until the house of God was built by Solomon [and] the ark passed from the tabernacle of skins into the temple constructed of stones; but that tabernacle which had been in the desert, and those skins which before the temple covered the roofs, were wonderful in their ministry. Indeed in the Song of Songs the bride praises her beginnings thus: *I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tabernacle of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon* (Song 1:4). And in another psalm, although David longed for the courts of the Lord, he nevertheless praises his tabernacles too, saying: *How wonderful [are your tabernacles], Lord; my soul longs for the courts of the Lord* (Ps. 83:2). For the tabernacle of God is indeed wonderful; but the house of God is more to be longed for. Indeed David himself too, when the kingdom of Israel was now at peace, while the ark of God remained in Zion under the skins of the tabernacle, longed to build the house of God. But what did the prophet say to him? *You shall not build me a house* (2 Sam. 7:7): it is not for everyone to build the house of God. So, as if towards greater ascents, we must make our passing over in the place of the tabernacle, so that we may come even to the house of God. And we are reminded by the example of Jerusalem that the house of the Lord is not built until the enemy and sin have been conquered; but yet we are in the tabernacle so long as the desert is being crossed, and until the land of the Jordan, the beginning of the promised inheritance, is entered, [and] every Canaanite enemy is subdued.

6. Now the difference between the dignity of the tabernacle and that of the house is this: in the tabernacle one does not always dwell, but in the house always, as David signifies in the [psalms of] ascents, saying: *For the Lord has chosen Zion, he has been pleased with it as a dwelling for himself: this is my rest for ever and ever* (Ps. 131:13). But in the tabernacle he has no rest: for it must be moved in time of war, when also the cloud which signified the presence of God would withdraw from it. This likeness will rightly be compared to us: so long as we are pilgrims in this body, let us in this equanimity conquer all its vices, so that no enemy is left alive or strong. For God will visit us even in the tabernacle, and in a time of quiet; but when a fight with the vices has arisen, our tabernacle must be packed up and made ready for a campaign of war; nor can it be spread out, nor take delight in the rest of God, at the time when the assault of the vices occurs. And God will indeed go before you in the fight, so that if you walk after him you may easily conquer your enemies; but he cannot dwell in you at that time. So, although you conquer, although you overcome the vices of the flesh, yet from the very struggle you stain your hands in your own blood. Nor will you be fit at this time to build the house of the Lord, just as David was rejected because he had worked in blood. But he builds the house of the Lord who enters into rest, who is troubled by no vices, for whom every enemy has been destroyed, who can say: *But the world is crucified to me and I to the world* (Gal. 6:14); with whom all old things have passed away [and] new things have been made, such as the kingdom of Solomon is taken to be as a figure of us. But if in the course of this life no one is found so perfect that he could come into the house of God clean from every assault of sin, I can nevertheless say this: *For I shall pass over into the place of the tabernacle, even to the house of God*; that is, in this present life, so that as long as I am in this world I pass over into the place of the tabernacle, since every day a fight must be waged against flesh and blood, against the spiritual forces of wickedness. But when the dwelling of this tabernacle has been dissolved, as the Apostle says, and [I] receive a house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens; when the body of our lowliness has been transfigured into the likeness of the body of the Son of God: then I shall come into the house of God, at which time he can dwell in me for ever; and rightly shall I sing: *For I shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.*

7. And this passing over of mine will be *with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting*. Nor is it any wonder if the shadow of the good things to come held an image of this joy, whether when David, moving the ark of God from the tabernacle of Zion, entered Jerusalem with dancing and drums, keeping a feast day, or when Solomon, having built the temple, brought in all the ministry with great exultation of those singing and making music to God. Nor is it any wonder, I say, when each of us exchanges this tabernacle of his body for that house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens, if his passing over is *with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting*.

8. So he who has received this hope rightly addressed the sadness of his soul, saying, verse 6: *Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.* And see whether it does not fit this understanding which we have followed, that in a time of persecution and of reproach for the name of God the righteous man should console his soul with a hope of this kind: *Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him.* But since it cannot be that one who casts his soul into death should not be troubled by some sadness, seeing that the Lord of all powers himself, the prince of faith himself, the Son of God himself, who before he came to the time of the cross spoke with such confidence as to say: *No one shall take my soul from me; I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again* (John 10:18); yet he too, in the hour close to death, said: *My soul is troubled even to death* (Mark 14:34); and: *Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me* (Matt. 26:39); and in his last groan: *God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* (Matt. 27:46). So this psalm too, showing in order the image of persecution, how great struggles and tribulations must be endured by the righteous man, through which his faith is to be tested and proved, therefore says, verse 7: *My God, my soul is troubled within me.* For who is there whose soul is not troubled in a time when men persecute the name of God? For besides that necessity of human frailty, besides bodily fears, there is a certain trouble peculiar to faith, when the persecutors of the name of God seem to grow and to rule, and God seems not to avenge his servants, nor to come to the aid of their tribulations, nor to stretch out his mighty right hand against his enemies. And therefore, since no one in a time of this kind keeps hold of the sense of God's judgements, that cry of the Lord is beautiful: *God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* (ibid.), by which he shows that he does not understand the reason why he has been forsaken. And if that master of wisdom and declarer of the Father, the Son, is so troubled as to ask the Father why he had forsaken him, what will the rest do, however righteous, when the depths of God's judgements come upon them? Yet the psalm teaches what alone we ought to hold fast to and do in these troubles. For every righteous man, when he is tempted, when he is afflicted, when he is in straits, when he comes into trouble of soul, even if he does not understand why these things befall him, must nevertheless not abandon faith nor condemn belief, which the prophet taught when he said: *Therefore I shall remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon, from the little mountain.* For because *my soul is troubled within me, therefore*, he says, *I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon*. For by the land of the Jordan he signifies the entrance of the promised inheritance for the people of Israel. And since we, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, consider faith to be the entrance of our inheritance — for this is the gate of our promises — therefore where the Prophet wished to commend the beginning of our faith, there he named the land of the Jordan and Mount Hermon. So too in the Song of Songs, where the first calling of the Church is made: *Come*, it says, *from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon* (Song 4:8): *passing over you will pass over, and you will pass over from the beginning of faith, from the head of Hermon.* Nor let it disturb anyone that in this place Senir is also named, since Mount Senir is the same as Hermon, which history, through Moses in Deuteronomy, teaches was situated in the land of the Jordan: *And we took*, it says, *at that time the land out of the hands of the two kings of the Amorites who were beside the Jordan, from the torrent to Hermon Senir* (Deut. 3:8). The Amorite called it Senir. So the head of Hermon, which is in the land of the Jordan, is called the beginning of faith. That is why there John the first forerunner is heard, and to John Christ is first shown; there the Lord is filled with the Holy Spirit, there the testimony of the Father's voice is given: *This is my Son in whom I am well pleased* (Matt. 3:17). From here, going forth, he is believed to have worked the beginnings of mighty deeds, here the beginnings of the signs by which the Son of God is believed.

9. Rightly, then, the head of Hermon is called the beginning of faith: from which we ought to remember our God, the salvation of our countenance, whenever our soul is troubled in temptations. For the beginning of faith is the first simple believing, the way by which we enter into faith in God through Jesus Christ. But wisdom is sought among the perfect (1 Cor. 2:6): what the varieties of God's judgments are, what the depths of his thoughts are. So, even if in the time of persecutions, in the turmoil of impending death, wisdom fails, let the beginning of faith not be abandoned; rather let us at least remember God with that simple and bare believing, knowing that the enemy has no power over us except so far as he is permitted. Yet let us not make use of the boasting of the foolish woman, by which it was said: *Where are the works of God's righteousness? Job, what did the fear of the Lord profit [you]?* (Job 22:3). But whenever the thought comes into this turmoil, it will be right, according to the teaching of this psalm, to say: *My God, my soul is troubled; therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon, from the little mountain.* So it is also with meaning that he adds the name 'little' to Mount Hermon: for the beginning of faith is a small mountain, and for one who has many ascents up to the kingdom of heaven, through insults, through injuries, through tribulations, through the death of the cross, believing in God is the first ascent. For whenever on that most bitter summit of the cross my soul is troubled, from the beginning of faith, from the little mountain, I will remember, Lord, you who are the salvation of my countenance.

10. *For deep calls on deep at the voice of your cataracts*, that is, the channels of God's testing, which the earth will undergo: for who has known the depths of his thoughts and judgments? The mind of the Lord is a flood, whose greatness the righteous man wishes to show, since he was speaking of his own tribulations: *Deep*, he says (v. 8), *calls on deep, at the voice of his cataracts.*

11. *All your heights and your waves have passed over me.* He gives the reason why his soul is troubled: for *deep calls on deep at the voice of the cataracts*. We have already said beforehand what we took the deep to be; yet we give the reason from what the prophet himself says: *Your judgments, Lord, are a great deep* (Ps. 35:7): for there is a great depth in the height of God's judgments, as if against us so often that judgment follows on judgment; what flesh could rise out [of it], what flesh endure [it]? See the Apostle: although he was treating [of it] in peace, yet, gazing on the mystery of God, he cries out, troubled: *O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable his judgments, how inscrutable his ways!* (Rom. 11:33). This depth of God's heart, then, is rightly named a deep, whose bottom no one knows: for there are many depths where there is no end. And rightly here *deep calls* us *on deep at the voice of your cataracts*. Let us set out certain kinds of deeps, so that the discussion may be clearer. See, the Son of God, coming with many signs and mighty deeds, heals the various sicknesses of many, and is accused of performing healings. Who was ever ill spoken of for having done good? And the Father allows so impious an insult to his Son: see, one deep. The judgments of God are set in motion, false witnesses are procured as though against a blasphemer and an irreligious man, when he alone was the true witness of God: and the impious give testimony, and win the case: see, a second deep follows the first. He is struck with fists, scourged, decked out in a mocking garment, the enemy exults and sneers, all impiety passes at length upon the Son of God: see, now a third deep is called upon [the others]; the Lord of glory is condemned on the cross, reckoned among thieves and the impious. See how many judgments the deep follows, so that it could rightly be said by him: *All your heights and your waves have passed over me.*

12. And here, I think, enough has now been said. But so that no one may ask, and think that we have passed over on purpose, what it means that he says: *At the voice of your cataracts deep calls on deep*, let us take up briefly the voice of the cataracts. These visible cataracts of waters certainly have their voices, because the outpourings of rivers must sound and roar. And whenever rivers rise to their outlet from a boundless lake of pools, or from the gushing of springs, whose depth can never fail or be exhausted, it is well said of them: *deep calls on deep at the voice of the cataracts*. But we ought to remember what deeps the prophet is speaking of, of which we too spoke beforehand. And so we ought to know their cataracts as well: we find that all the outpourings of God's judgments sounded through the voices of the prophets, which I think are here called cataracts. *Deep calls on deep at the voice of the cataracts.* After the preaching of the prophets the judgments of God followed, and as it were called themselves into that voice which had gone before so that they might follow. A voice of the cataract was: *Let us oppress the righteous man, because he is useless to us, and opposed to our works, and calls himself Son of God* (Wis. 2:12). Another voice of the cataract is: *Like a sheep he was led to the sacrifice, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth* (Isa. 53:7). There is also another voice: *They dug my hands and my feet, they counted all my bones* (Ps. 21:17). There is also that voice: *They divided my garments, and over my garment they cast lots* (ibid. 19); *and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink* (Ps. 68:22). And what need is there now to recount all the voices of the cataracts, when the books of the prophets are full of the insults and passion of the Lord? Since, then, the reality of things accomplished followed upon all the preachings, deep called on deep into this voice of the cataracts, so that, that is, the outcome might fulfil their sounds. Therefore, since the prophet was speaking of such deeps, he fittingly adds and says:

13. Vv. 9 and 10. *By day the Lord has commanded his mercy, and by night he has made [it] manifest: with me is my prayer to the God of my life: I will say to God, You are my upholder, why have you forgotten?* He clearly gives teaching and consolation to all the righteous, that if, covered by many waves of temptations, they suffer turmoil of mind, which, as a darkness of the eyes, is called night, they should remember that the mercy of God is always made manifest in this night, mighty, unless the time is [not] a cause for showing mercy. But when we have come into danger, and turmoil from despair of life has made a kind of night in our heart, then if we can say: *With me is prayer to my God: I will say, You are my upholder, why have you forsaken me?* This, then, must be held fast in the night; and when the other senses are troubled, yet this ought not to fail, that we cry to the Lord: *why have you forsaken me?* a saying we treated earlier: for even if, by reason of God's judgments, we do not understand why he leaves us in certain temptations, we must nevertheless not fail to beg mercy from him.

14. *Why*, he says, *do I go about sad, while the enemy afflicts me* (v. 11) *and breaks my bones?* This, then, will always be the prayer of the righteous man, even in the night. And as for his saying: *He breaks my bones*, death close at hand is certainly not to be understood; but since here his patience was being broken in tribulation, which is the support and strength of our mind as the bones are of the body, he called patience 'bones', which is broken by constant tribulations: *while you break*, he says, *my bones, those who trouble me reproached [me], saying daily: Where is your God?* But although the righteous man feels this heavy hand, he nevertheless teaches what must be done, and what remedy is to be held to in persecutions, saying (v. 12): *Why are you sad, my soul, why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.* With this example set before us, if any vexation, if any pressure, if any reproach of the name of God comes upon us, if our soul is sad, if it is troubled, let us say: *Hope in God, for I will confess to him*, under the protection of Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
